items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks: up to 4 for indicative content plus up to 2 for structure and linkages. Key points: methane has only London forces; London forces are weaker than hydrogen bonds; NH3, H2O and HF have hydrogen bonds; London forces are similar because the electron numbers are the same; F is the most electronegative so the H-F bond is the most polar; water has more hydrogen bonds per molecule (2:1) than NH3 or HF, hence the highest boiling temperature.

items.name: Intermolecular forces in liquefying hydrogen and ammonia
items.how: Level-of-response (*) question: compare and contrast the intermolecular forces involved when hydrogen and ammonia liquefy, describing how these forces are formed.
items.ms: Level of response, 6 marks (up to 4 for indicative points plus 2 for structure and reasoning). Similarity: both form London forces, from a temporary dipole inducing a dipole in a neighbouring molecule, smaller in H2 because it has few electrons and its electron cloud is not easily polarised. Difference: ammonia forms hydrogen bonds between the N lone pair and the delta-plus H of another molecule (N very electronegative), and hydrogen bonds are stronger than London forces so ammonia liquefies more easily.

items.ms: Indicative points: nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis); silver halide precipitate forms; rate depends on C-halogen bond strength; C-X bond strength falls down Group 7 so the iodo compound is fastest; reactivity 1 degree < 2 degree < 3 degree; identification of the primary, secondary and tertiary compounds. items.name: Methanol from CO2: equilibrium, oxidation, carbon neutrality
items.how: Context question on CO2 + 3H2 <-> CH3OH + H2O (dH = -49.5 kJ mol-1, 50 atm, 250 C, copper catalyst): only (a)(i) 'explain why high pressure is used' is printed in the input; the MS also covers conditions and catalyst, oxidation of methanol, a functional-group test, IR evidence, and carbon neutrality with a CO2 mass calculation.
items.ms: (a)(i) fewer gas moles on the right so high pressure favours methanol (or more collisions raise the rate); (ii) exothermic so low temperature favours yield, a compromise temperature gives a fast enough rate; (iii) catalyst allows lower temperature or is selective/reusable. (b) acidified dichromate under reflux, CH3OH + 2[O] -> HCOOH + H2O, effervescence with carbonate, IR loss of O-H (3750-3200) and C=O (1725-1700) appears. (c) CO2 captured would have been released anyway, 8 x 44 = 352 g CO2 per mole of octane, 5% of 1200 kg petrol gives 185 kg CO2 saved.
